text:
*Interview with Dr Casimir Vauthier, in the dining room. Second interview of the night.*

MATTHEY: Good evening, Doctor. Please sit down. I am sorry to keep you from your bed.

DR VAUTHIER: Good evening, Inspector. I doubt I shall be of much use, but I will answer what I can. Do you mind if I light a cigar? Aurèle would have scolded me for sitting in his dining room without one.

MATTHEY: Not at all.

DR VAUTHIER: Thank you. I have been this family's doctor and friend for as long as I can remember. I attended Jules Monnier, Aurèle's brother, in his last illness, in 1889. Félix's father. I did not like what I saw then, and I did not like what I saw tonight. I tell you so that you understand I am no stranger to this house, and that I know its griefs.

MATTHEY: Tell me about dinner, if you would.

DR VAUTHIER: Aurèle has done the same thing every New Year's Eve since I have known him. When the temple bell struck nine, he made us all show him our watches, and then he told each of us what was wrong with ours. He could never leave a watch alone. Mine was two minutes ahead of the bell. He saw it at once, and he said so.

MATTHEY: And after dinner?

DR VAUTHIER: Madame and I played piquet in the salon. Odile plays a better game than she admits. We played until a quarter to eleven by my watch, when I went out to the hall to fetch my cigar case from my coat. Madame began to play the piano as I went out, and she stopped when I came back.

MATTHEY: Did you look at a clock while you were playing?

DR VAUTHIER: Yes. When the temple struck ten during our game, I looked at the salon clock. It showed five minutes to ten. I remarked on it to Madame.

MATTHEY: Thank you. You have examined Aurèle?

DR VAUTHIER: I have. The blow was to the back of the head. A man struck like that would have known very little about it. It would have been very quick. I can say no more than that, Inspector, and I would not wish to say more than I know.

MATTHEY: I understand. Did you notice anything about the atelier?

DR VAUTHIER: The regulator on the wall had stopped. I thought, God forgive me, that it had stopped with its master. It is a foolish thing to think, and I am a foolish old man for thinking it. He had his repeater in his hand. He was so proud of that watch. Four years of his life went into it, and he never once let anyone hurry him.

MATTHEY: You knew his work well?

DR VAUTHIER: I knew his temper better. He could be cruel about a watch and kind about a person, which is rarer. *De mortuis nil nisi bonum.* I have been trying all evening to remember the rest of that sentence, and I cannot, which seems fitting for a physician.

MATTHEY: Is there anything you have not told me that you think I should know?

DR VAUTHIER: Only that I am tired, Inspector, and that I have lost a friend. I would have said that before you asked me, if you had let me.

MATTHEY: Then I will let you go soon. Thank you, Doctor.

DR VAUTHIER: Thank you. You are kinder than I expected. Please forgive me the cigar; I shall not light it now.
